title: Of days and seasons
sentences: Of days and seasons
The wood was sombre, the sky was black; night, without comfort or stars,
had sunk down from infinity upon all that was mortal in the world — when the little boy woke.
He was a child of a few years; in the forest he had been abandoned or lost — he himself no longer remembered,
because he had slept so long — days.
Trembling with his great frightened eyes, he looked about,
and nowhere among the trees could he find the path: black was all he saw.
`Where am I?'
thought the boy.
`And who am I, and where must I go ...'
He remembered vaguely something of light or warmth,
like a mirage from a sun-palace — but no more than a mirage did he remember, and now that he was fully awake he became aware only
that he was abandoned, lost in a wood of terror, and the mirage was gone.
Then the little boy began to weep in childish despair.
He was afraid of beasts and of robbers ...
And when he saw something dimly approaching him, he thought it was the wild man,
and felt himself already dying, while his little heart beat in his throat and his eyes bulged in horror.
But the dim shape was not the wild man; the dim shape was a white woman ...
The little boy, in his mirage of memory from the sun-palace, even believed he recognized her: a woman
wholly white as he remembered white women, and in both fear and expectation the little boy went toward her.
`White woman ...!'
begged the child, and folded his hands in a gesture of prayer
that had perhaps been taught him, in the sun-palace, long ago ...
The white woman was tall and slender, and her white veils were
the only whiteness in the sombre wood, against the black depth of the forest.
She bent over the child, and her gaze struck him from between her veils, which her white hands parted briefly,
as if she wished to see better; her gaze came from deep dark eyes, eyes as deep and dark as the wood ...
`White woman ...!'
the child repeated pleadingly.
`Who are you, my child?'
asked the white woman, in a deep dark voice.
`And whence do you come, and whither must you go?'
He began to weep again, the small boy, for the woman's voice frightened him and he did not know who he was,
whence he came, or even whither he must go ...
`Then come with me!'
said the white woman softly and gravely, and she stretched out her hand.
The little boy gave her his little hand, and walked now beside her, still weeping.
`Weep no more,' said the white woman.
`See, you go quite safely by my hand; let me lead you: do not be afraid.
In this wood there are no beasts or robbers.'
The child felt a gentle trust, especially now that the cold hand of the white woman grew warm from his glowing child's hand,
yet still he stumbled very often and his short legs grew weary.
`Let me carry you then, my darling ...'
She lifted the weary child to her breast,
and carried him very lightly between her white veils: with inaudible step she went on ...
In her arms the child fell asleep, and dreamed of sun-glory and white women, and also of white little children ...
When it woke, the child smiled and looked at its bearer in the deep dark eyes.
`You are a good white woman, are you not?'
asked the child full of trust, and clasped its arms around her neck.
`Yes,' answered the white woman, `I am a good white woman, my child.'
`Are you not weary of carrying me, good white woman?'
`No, my child, I do not grow weary ...
I never rest, I always go ...'
`Always?'
`Always ...'
`Through the whole wood?'
`Through the whole wood ...
See, the morning pales between the branches, and marks the way more clearly.'
`Now I can walk again, white woman ...'
The white woman set him down, carefully on his little feet, wrapping herself deeper in her veils.
The child walked on beside her, glad now that all night's mystery was resolved in the laughing morning.
`Oh,' cried the child; `see what a beautiful flower ...'
`And there, what a beautiful chapel!'
`Oh!'
the child rejoiced.
`I should like to have them: chapel and flower both ...'
`Then I shall give you chapel and flower,' said the white woman; `but then you must give me something in return.'
`And what can I give you, white woman?'
`In return for chapel and flower, my child, give me this morning hour.'
`Oh, splendid is the flower, and splendid is the chapel: oh,
white woman, I gladly give you this morning hour in return ...'
The white woman smiled, and with deep dark gaze she looked down upon the greedy child ...
Then she caught the butterfly in her veil, and bent over the abyss to pluck the blue flower.
And both she offered the child, who rejoiced with happiness ...
`Oh, white woman, oh white woman!'
rejoiced the happy child.
`How happy I am with my flower and my butterfly!'
But in his joy the boy crushed the butterfly dead and the flower withered in his little hand.
`How soon, oh white woman, my flower has withered and my little butterfly is dead!'
`But, dear child, butterflies do not live long, especially not in children's hands, and flowers wither even faster ...
But if you give me this new spring day, I shall conjure along all your way today a thousand butterflies and a thousand flowers.'
`A thousand butterflies, and a thousand flowers!!
Oh, white woman, for so many flowers and butterflies I gladly give in return my spring day.'
Now the sun had burst forth wholly in splendour, and the wood was no longer black night, but shone spring-green, spring-gold ...
And along the radiant way the child walked spring-drunken,
and plucked flowers and caught moths, for it bloomed and fluttered along the whole way.
But in the evening the flowers had withered and all the moths were dead.
`yet it was a delightful spring day!'
the child exulted with already sleep-drunken eyes, and wearily clasped its arms around the white woman,
and fell asleep at her heart, between her veils.
Night fell, the white woman walked on, and her deep-dark eyes smiled mournfully.
`But that delightful spring day now ...
is mine!'
murmured the white woman, in deep-dark voice.
The white woman brought the little boy into the city among other people and children, and the child grew up there,
and became tall and strong among those he thought his parents, his brothers and sisters, kinsmen and friends.
After years the white woman appeared to him again, whom he had wholly forgotten,
and whose deep-dark eyes frightened him, even though he was now a young man of eighteen years.
`My son!'
the white woman called him.
`I have not forgotten you.'
`I was ungrateful, white woman,' confessed the young man.
`White woman, you saved me, a lost and abandoned child, from the sombre wood of night ...
And you gave me butterflies and flowers ...'
`Thousands ...
for one spring day!'
Yes ...
thousands ...
for one spring day.
You brought me into the city among those who would have been my parents ...'
`And fed and cared for you, until you became a man, my son, young man of eighteen years.
But do you not remember the promise, what you would give me for those countless kindnesses ...'
`Yes, white woman, as clearly as the spring day in return for the butterflies and flowers,
I remember the eighteen spring seasons that you demanded to bring me into the city among those who would be my parents,
and would raise me with brothers and sisters, and would let me live with kinsmen and friends.'
`If you still remember that promise, my son, the white woman is content ...
And she is happy that for eighteen spring seasons, for what is so little,
and so ethereal, and so fading, you have received: youth, and a young man's time of pure happiness.'
`But now, white woman, my happiness is past and I suffer bitter grief.
For I love a girl so beautiful and so good,
as no other girl in the world lives, and I would call her my wife ...
But she does not love me, and my possessions are few,
and my only comfort is none other than my sorrow, when I pour it out upon my violin ...'
`My son, you know how dearly I love you.
If you give me in return for the bride you desire, and the gold that will make you respected among men,
no more than twenty blooming summers, then I gladly grant you your happiness, a wife and wealth.
But lament no more in music, for even more ethereal and fleeting
than what I ever asked of you, spring days and summer months, is music, which fades into nothing ...'
`Yet music has comforted me, white woman.'
`Live the happiness, my son, with what I give you, wife and gold ...'
`Oh, white woman, oh white woman, for so much would I not give all my blooming summers ...'
The white woman looked at the young man with deep dark eyes, and for years she did not return.
He married the wife he so ardently desired, and in the slowly turning years he came to esteem, riches and power,
until war broke out, and stirred the land, and the smoke of burning cities darkened sky and horizon.
Then the white woman appeared before her foster-son for the third time, and she seemed to become terrible to him,
her face thin and hollow, bony her arm, and skeletal her threatening hand.
`Oh, white woman, oh white woman!'
cried out passionately the man whose care already wrinkled his face, whose ambition scorched his soul.
`Years ago you offered me happiness for twenty summers.
But happiness I have never found ...
When the flower and the butterfly died, my love died and withered too, and my gold never became my happiness.
Now I wish only to be wholly mighty, for supreme power must surely be happiness,
and a crown I wish pressed upon my temples.'
`Foster-son,' said the white woman; `my dear child, whom I never forgot: if you give me in return for the crown of this land fifty purple autumn seasons,
I shall bring about a fortunate chance in the war that makes you ruler over these cities.'
The ambitious man accepted the bargain hastily, and a terrible battle raged for seven days.
The battlefields lay strewn with corpses: death seemed to rule almighty.
The white woman's foster-son had taken a sword in hand; he fought in the foremost ranks,
and a mysterious power seemed to protect him in the heat of battle and make him invulnerable ...
He, at the head of the country's troops, won the victory, and they pressed the crown upon his head ...
And he grew old under the weight of that crown, until war raged again,
revolt broke out, and abandoned by all his own, wretched and half naked, he fled,
and fell in the same sombre wood where he as a forsaken little boy had been found by the white woman.
Old and wretched he lay down in the twilight of the sinking evening, when she appeared before him as a terror:
grey hair tangled wildly about her face, which grinned like a death's-head and in which hollow eyes were sunk.
`Oh white woman, oh white woman!'
cried out the unhappy king: `with a crown you thought to give me happiness, and turned the chance of war in my favour,
in return for fifty purple autumn seasons, but nothing but care has my crown brought me;
happiness I have never known save perhaps that very first spring day when you conjured butterflies and flowers for me!
And yet you were my life!
Why have you been so cruel!
Oh white woman, oh white woman ...
now that I lie here, wretched, abandoned, now I beg you alone, you
who are so mighty, give to my poor children, give to my wretched subjects ...
life and a glimpse of happiness ...
be it what it may ...
flower, butterfly, bride, gold, or crown ...'
`Oh my son, oh my son,' raged the white woman.
`Ungrateful you have always been.
You have counted neither flower, nor butterfly, nor bride, nor gold, nor crown.
But if you give me this last icy winter hour ...
then I grant your children and subjects life, and their glimpse of happiness.'
Now she helped him rise, and led him onward, for sobbing he had given her his last winter hour.
And she led him to a monument, of which she opened the bronze door.
`Go in,' she pointed threateningly; `that I may now receive all: all the spring days, summer and autumn seasons,
and also the last winter hour: all that you promised me in return for my countless kindnesses.'
The old king stumbled and reeled.
`This is a grave ...'
he said, looking up at the monument.
`This is a king's grave,' she answered.
`Tomorrow your panegyrists, oh son, will scratch words of glory that glorify you in transience.
Go in ...
that yonder I may receive what you owe me.'
She held open the bronze doors.
`Were you not then my life?'
asked the ruler on the threshold of the sepulchre.
`Oh, tell me ...
are you not life?'
`No,' said the white woman sombrely.
`I was never your life.
I am not life.
I am Death.'
And she bade him go within.
He obeyed; slowly she turned to the bronze door, which creaked on heavy hinges.
`And my life?'
his voice still pleaded, while fearfully the old king peered through the still open crack of the slowly closing tomb door.
`Come ...!'
said the white woman more softly.
`When you have first paid me your debt, of days and seasons ...'
Then she closed the door, for thousands of years.
De Gids 1901 IV, 191-203
